sentence: I need ___ pen to sign this form.
setupText: Choose the word that makes a grammatical sentence.
taskText: I need ___ pen to sign this form.
text: Choose the word that makes a grammatical sentence. I need ___ pen to sign this form.
explanation: Use 'a' before a singular countable noun beginning with a consonant sound: 'a pen'.

rationales.a: Use 'a' before a singular countable noun beginning with a consonant sound: 'a pen'.
rationales.an: Pen begins with the consonant sound /p/, so use a, not an.
rationales.these: 'These' refers to more than one thing; 'pen' is singular.

sentence: One ticket is for me and one is for my husband. I want ___ tickets, please.
setupText: Choose the number that matches the situation.
taskText: One ticket is for me and one is for my husband. I want ___ tickets, please.
text: Choose the number that matches the situation. One ticket is for me and one is for my husband. I want ___ tickets, please.
explanation: One ticket for each of two people makes two tickets.

rationales.three: Three would include one more ticket than the two people need.
rationales.two: One ticket for each of two people makes two tickets.
rationales.four: Four would give the two people two tickets each, not one.
rationales.ten: Ten is a different quantity; only two tickets are requested.

sentence: I cannot pay. I do not have ___ money.
setupText: Choose the word that makes a grammatical sentence.
taskText: I cannot pay. I do not have ___ money.
text: Choose the word that makes a grammatical sentence. I cannot pay. I do not have ___ money.
focusKey: coverage-determiners-and-quantifiers-a1-1083:Any with an uncountable noun after not
explanation: 'Not any money' means no money. 'Any' can go before the uncountable noun 'money'.

rationales.many: 'Many' goes with plural things we count, such as 'coins'; 'money' is uncountable.
rationales.a: We do not say a money for cash; use a coin or a note for one piece.
rationales.any: 'Not any money' means no money. 'Any' can go before the uncountable noun 'money'.
rationales.these: These needs a plural countable noun, such as notes, not money.

sentence: The cafe opens Monday to Sunday. It opens ___.
setupText: Choose the words that match the opening times.
taskText: The cafe opens Monday to Sunday. It opens ___.
text: Choose the words that match the opening times. The cafe opens Monday to Sunday. It opens ___.
explanation: Every day includes all seven days, matching Monday to Sunday.

rationales.one day a week: That describes one opening day, but the cafe opens on seven days.
rationales.on Mondays only: Only Mondays leaves out Tuesday to Sunday.
rationales.at weekends only: The cafe also opens from Monday to Friday.
rationales.every day: Every day includes all seven days, matching Monday to Sunday.

sentence: Please cut ___ for lunch.
setupText: Choose the words for an amount of food, without saying an exact amount.
taskText: Please cut ___ for lunch.
text: Choose the words for an amount of food, without saying an exact amount. Please cut ___ for lunch.
explanation: Some bread gives an amount without saying how many slices.

rationales.some bread: Some bread gives an amount without saying how many slices.
rationales.two slices of bread: This gives an exact number of slices; the request asks for no exact amount.
rationales.these bread: 'Bread' is not plural here, so 'these' cannot go directly before it.
rationales.many bread: Use 'many slices of bread' when counting slices; 'bread' itself is uncountable.

sentence: There is ___ email from the hotel in my inbox.
setupText: Choose the word that makes a grammatical sentence.
taskText: There is ___ email from the hotel in my inbox.
text: Choose the word that makes a grammatical sentence. There is ___ email from the hotel in my inbox.
explanation: Use an before the vowel sound at the start of email.

rationales.a: 'Email' starts with a vowel sound, so the article is 'an'.
rationales.an: Use an before the vowel sound at the start of email.
rationales.many: Many emails would need a plural noun and There are.
rationales.those: 'Those emails' is plural, but this sentence has 'is' and singular 'email'.

sentence: Look at ___ photo here in my hand.
setupText: Choose the word for one thing near the speaker.
taskText: Look at ___ photo here in my hand.
text: Choose the word for one thing near the speaker. Look at ___ photo here in my hand.
explanation: This points to one thing near the speaker, such as the photo in their hand.

rationales.these: 'These' is for more than one photo; 'photo' is singular.
rationales.that: That usually points to something farther away; the task asks for the near form.
rationales.this: This points to one thing near the speaker, such as the photo in their hand.
rationales.those: Those is for plural things farther away, not this one nearby photo.

sentence: Are ___ shoes here by my feet yours?
setupText: Choose the word for more than one thing near the speaker.
taskText: Are ___ shoes here by my feet yours?
text: Choose the word for more than one thing near the speaker. Are ___ shoes here by my feet yours?
explanation: These points to plural things near the speaker, here the shoes by their feet.

rationales.this: 'This' goes with one thing; 'shoes' is plural.
rationales.that: That is singular and does not match shoes.
rationales.those: 'Those' is the farther-away form; the task asks for the near form.
rationales.these: These points to plural things near the speaker, here the shoes by their feet.

sentence: ___ building over there is our hotel.
setupText: Choose the word for one thing far from the speaker.
taskText: ___ building over there is our hotel.
text: Choose the word for one thing far from the speaker. ___ building over there is our hotel.
explanation: That points to one thing farther away, matching building over there.

rationales.That: That points to one thing farther away, matching building over there.
rationales.This: This is the near form; the task asks for a distant building.
rationales.These: 'These' refers to several nearby things; 'building' is singular.
rationales.Those: 'Those' is the distant plural form, but only one building is named.

sentence: Can you read ___ signs over there, across the road?
setupText: Choose the word for several things far from the speaker.
taskText: Can you read ___ signs over there, across the road?
text: Choose the word for several things far from the speaker. Can you read ___ signs over there, across the road?
explanation: Those matches the plural signs and the distance across the road.

rationales.that: 'That' needs a singular noun such as 'sign'.
rationales.those: Those matches the plural signs and the distance across the road.
rationales.this: This is singular and near; neither matches the task.
rationales.these: 'These' is plural but points to nearby things; the signs are distant.

sentence: I live here. This is ___ address.
setupText: Choose the form used before a noun in modern standard written English.
taskText: I live here. This is ___ address.
text: Choose the form used before a noun in modern standard written English. I live here. This is ___ address.
explanation: 'My' goes before a noun to show that it belongs or relates to the speaker.

rationales.mine: Mine can stand alone, as in The address is mine; it does not go before address.
rationales.me: 'Me' is an object form, not a word showing whose address it is.
rationales.my: 'My' goes before a noun to show that it belongs or relates to the speaker.
rationales.I: 'I' is used as a subject, as in 'I live here', not before 'address'.

sentence: Sara cannot find ___ phone.
setupText: Choose the form used before a noun in standard written English.
taskText: Sara cannot find ___ phone.
text: Choose the form used before a noun in standard written English. Sara cannot find ___ phone.
explanation: Her goes before phone to show that the phone belongs to Sara.

rationales.hers: 'Hers' replaces a noun phrase, but 'phone' is still present.
rationales.she: 'She' is a subject form; use 'her' to show whose phone it is.
rationales.herself: Herself refers back to Sara as a person; it does not introduce phone.
rationales.her: Her goes before phone to show that the phone belongs to Sara.

sentence: We start work at nine. ___ first break is at eleven.
setupText: Choose the possessive form used in standard written English.
taskText: We start work at nine. ___ first break is at eleven.
text: Choose the possessive form used in standard written English. We start work at nine. ___ first break is at eleven.
explanation: Our goes before first break and shows that the break is for us.

rationales.Our: Our goes before first break and shows that the break is for us.
rationales.Ours: Ours stands alone; it cannot introduce first break.
rationales.Us: 'Us' is an object form, as in 'Tell us', not a possessive word before 'break'.
rationales.We: 'We' is a subject pronoun; 'Our first break' is the subject needed here.

sentence: I bought a bag yesterday. ___ bag is blue.
setupText: Choose the word that points back to the same bag.
taskText: I bought a bag yesterday. ___ bag is blue.
text: Choose the word that points back to the same bag. I bought a bag yesterday. ___ bag is blue.
explanation: The bag points back to the bag already introduced with a bag.

rationales.A: A bag would introduce a bag without clearly pointing back to the one just mentioned.
rationales.The: The bag points back to the bag already introduced with a bag.
rationales.An: Bag begins with a consonant sound, so an bag is incorrect.
rationales.Some: Some bag does not clearly identify the previously mentioned bag; use the for that reference.

sentence: My key box is empty. There are ___ keys in it.
setupText: Choose the word that means zero.
taskText: My key box is empty. There are ___ keys in it.
text: Choose the word that means zero. My key box is empty. There are ___ keys in it.
explanation: 'No keys' means zero keys, which matches an empty box.

rationales.some: 'Some keys' would mean that the box is not empty.
rationales.two: Two keys would be a positive number; the box has none.
rationales.no: 'No keys' means zero keys, which matches an empty box.
rationales.many: 'Many keys' means a large number, not an empty box.

sentence: The bread shop is open and the fruit shop is open. ___ shops are open.
setupText: Choose the word that includes the two shops.
taskText: The bread shop is open and the fruit shop is open. ___ shops are open.
text: Choose the word that includes the two shops. The bread shop is open and the fruit shop is open. ___ shops are open.
explanation: Both means the two together: the bread shop and the fruit shop.

rationales.One: 'One' needs singular 'shop' and does not include the two shops.
rationales.No: No shops are open would mean the two shops are closed.
rationales.Every: 'Every' takes a singular noun: 'every shop'. It cannot go before 'shops'.
rationales.Both: Both means the two together: the bread shop and the fruit shop.

sentence: This road is busy. There are ___ buses.
setupText: Choose the words that make a grammatical sentence.
taskText: This road is busy. There are ___ buses.
text: Choose the words that make a grammatical sentence. This road is busy. There are ___ buses.
explanation: 'A lot of buses' means a large number of buses; keep 'of' before the noun.

rationales.a lot of: 'A lot of buses' means a large number of buses; keep 'of' before the noun.
rationales.a lot: 'A lot' needs 'of' when a noun follows: 'a lot of buses'.
rationales.much: 'Much' goes with uncountable nouns; 'buses' are countable and plural.
rationales.many of: 'Many of' needs a word such as 'the' before 'buses': 'many of the buses'.

sentence: How ___ emails did you send today?
setupText: Choose the word that makes a grammatical question.
taskText: How ___ emails did you send today?
text: Choose the word that makes a grammatical question. How ___ emails did you send today?
explanation: How many asks for the number of plural countable things, here emails.

rationales.much: 'Much' asks about an uncountable amount; individual emails can be counted.
rationales.many: How many asks for the number of plural countable things, here emails.
rationales.some: How some does not form a question about a number.
rationales.any: How any is not the quantity-question pattern; use how many emails.

sentence: How ___ rent do you pay each month?
setupText: Choose the word that makes a grammatical question.
taskText: How ___ rent do you pay each month?
text: Choose the word that makes a grammatical question. How ___ rent do you pay each month?
explanation: 'How much' asks for an amount; 'rent' here is an amount of money.

rationales.many: 'Rent' is an amount of money here, not plural things to count.
rationales.a: How a rent is not a question about an amount.
rationales.much: 'How much' asks for an amount; 'rent' here is an amount of money.
rationales.every: 'Every' refers to all members of a group and cannot follow 'how' in this amount question.

sentence: Four people want tea. We have only three cups. We ___.
setupText: Choose the words that match the situation.
taskText: Four people want tea. We have only three cups. We ___.
text: Choose the words that match the situation. Four people want tea. We have only three cups. We ___.
explanation: 'Enough' means as many as needed. Three cups are not enough for four people.

rationales.have no cups: There are three cups, so the number is not zero.
rationales.have four cups: The sentence says there are three cups, not four.
rationales.have enough cups: One cup per person needs four cups; three is too few.
rationales.do not have enough cups: 'Enough' means as many as needed. Three cups are not enough for four people.
